newsitem.title: USA: Sony studio chief Levine resigns.
newsitem.headline: Sony studio chief Levine resigns.

text.p: Sony Corp. said Wednesday that Alan Levine resigned from as president and chief operating officer of Sony Pictures Entertainment, ending weeks of speculation about his future at the troubled studio.
In a terse statement, Sony said Levine agreed to stay on for a brief period of time to assist the management transition at Sony Pictures.
Sony did not name a replacement for Levine but the company has been reportedly in talks with United Artists President John Calley about taking the top studio job.

"We greatly appreciate Alan's leadership of SPE over the past two years, as well as his long term contribution to Sony," said Nobuyuki Idei, president and chief operating officer of Sony Corp. "He has been instrumental in a complex transition and restructuring at SPE, and has solidly positioned the studio for the next stage in its worldwide growth and evolution," he said.
Levine's departure had been rumoured for months after Sony's dismal performance at the box office this summer.
In recent weeks, rumours of Levine's pending departure intensified despite numerous efforts by the company to put a stop to them.

In September, Levine fired studio boss Mark Canton. However, his choice for Canton's replacement, William Morris talent agent Arnold Rifkin, was voted down by Idei, prompting many in Hollywood to suggest Levine's tenure at Sony was short-lived.
Canton's departure was the latest in a series of high-level resignations at the studio, which Sony purchased in 1989 for $3.4 billion.

Earlier this summer, Marc Platt, president of Sony's TriStar Pictures, left to take a job at Universal Pictures and Lisa Henson, president of Sony's Columbia Pictures, stepped down to form her own production company.
In addition, Sid Ganis, the head of Sony Pictures marketing unit, also stepped down.

Analysts said Levine, a former entertainment lawyer, earned high marks for cutting Sony's costs and restoring the studio to profitability. The studio's lack of box office hits, however, put pressure on Levine.
Several Sony films did poorly at the box office this summer, including "The Fan", "The Cable Guy" and "Multiplicity".
"The Cable Guy" was a particularly embarrassing film for Sony because the studio had paid comedian Jim Carrey $20 million to star in the film and the studio spent millions more to promote it.
